summary: Expands on an experimental Encoding header field for Internet mail that supports multi-part, multi-structured messages. It replaces RFC 1154.

plainLanguage.summary: A parcel can hold several things at once. This memo adds a label to an email telling the reader how the parts inside were packed.

questions: encoding header field for internet mail
what is the rfc 1505 encoding header
how does the encoding header field work in email
what replaced the encoding header field
subtitle: An experimental mail header that describes how each part of a message body is encoded, without changing the body.

tldr.problem: An RFC 822 message has one header and one body, so there is no standard way to say that a body holds several parts with different encodings.
tldr.mechanism: An Encoding header lists one subfield per body part, each with an optional line count and one or more keywords such as Text, uuencode, PGP or LZJU90. The RFC also defines the FS and LZJU90 encodings in full.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental protocol that replaces RFC 1154, and an IESG note says a standards-track technology already exists in this area.

today: RFC 1505 is Experimental and replaces RFC 1154. Its own IESG note says that a standards-track technology already exists in this area, citing RFC 1341 (MIME).

sections.title: Splitting a Message Body into Parts
sections.content:
RFC 822 defines a mail message as a header and a body separated by a blank line. The Encoding header field lets the body itself be broken into parts, each separated from the next by a blank line. Each part has an encoding type, and the default with no Encoding field is a single part of type Text.

The aim is to describe the content without putting constraints or extra structure in the body that could interfere with other processing. The RFC says the field is even more useful in network news, where articles are often uuencoded or shar'd and keep their structure information in the usually hidden header.
sections.plainLanguage: A letter can have several pages. The label on the envelope says how many lines each page has and what kind of page it is.

sections.title: The Encoding Field Syntax
sections.content:
The field is a comma-separated list of subfields, one per message part in order. Each subfield is a line count and one or more keywords. The count is a non-negative decimal number of text lines in the part, may be zero, and is optional on the last part. A count always starts with a digit and a keyword always starts with a letter, so the two can be told apart.

Keywords are not case-sensitive. A series of nested keywords is read left to right. A decoder processes them in that order, while an encoder generates them in the reverse of the order in which it applied the encodings. Comments in parentheses may appear anywhere, may be passed to clients, and must not be used for interpreting content.
sections.plainLanguage: The label lists the parts in order. Each one has a line count and a word naming how it was packed, and if it was packed more than once the words are listed in order.

sections.title: Defined Encoding Keywords
sections.content:
The RFC defines keywords including Text, Message, Hex, EVFU, EDI-X12, EDIFACT, FS, LZJU90, LZW, UUENCODE, PEM, PEM-Clear, PGP, Signature, TAR, PostScript, SHAR and URL. Message marks a part that is itself an Internet message. Signature must always be nested after another keyword, as in 14 Text, 3 Text Signature.

For privacy, the sender can use PGP Message so an eavesdropper cannot see the nested type. The RFC warns that a decoder should not automatically execute decoded shell archive statements, and says the use of shar is supported but not recommended.

New keywords must be registered with IANA, and keywords starting with X- are permanently reserved for implementation-specific use. Registrations must reference a non-Internet standard or an existing or soon to be RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a list of words for common ways of packing things, like plain text, zipped, or secret. Anyone can add a new word if they ask the official keeper of lists.

sections.title: File System Object Encoding
sections.content:
The FS encoding moves a structured set of files from one environment to another while keeping common attributes. It is built from nested sections that start with [ and a directive keyword and end with ]. The section keywords are directory, entry, file, segment and data. The data section must be last within its container.

Attributes come before sub-sections and include display, type, created, modified, accessed, owner, group, acl, password, block, record and application. A Macintosh file is encoded with its two forks as segments. Dates look like 15 Apr 1993 20:05:22.12 -0500. The RFC says a password in plain text is not considered a security problem here, because the file content follows anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a way to pack a whole folder, with each file's name, dates and owner, into one email so it can be unpacked just as it was.

sections.title: LZJU90 Compression
sections.content:
LZJU90 compresses a binary or text object with a modified LZ77 method, then writes each 6 bits of output as a text character from a 64-character set made of the plus sign, the hyphen, the digits, and upper-case and lower-case letters, chosen to survive code translations such as ASCII to EBCDIC. The text starts with an identifying line made of an asterisk, LZJU90 and an optional name, and ends with a line giving the original byte count and an 8-digit hexadecimal CRC.

The compressed data mixes literal characters and copy pointers. The minimum copy length is 3 and the maximum is 256, and the maximum offset is 32255. Lengths and offsets use start-step-stop unary codes. Compression is defined by the decoder, so any encoder whose output decodes correctly is valid. The RFC gives a C decoder, an example encoder, and a sample compressed object. It also states the worst case as a 1/8 increase in size, or 3/2 of the original after character encoding.

Lines are recommended to break every 78 characters, and a decoder must accept lines of 1 to 1000 characters.
sections.plainLanguage: It squeezes a file by saying 'same as before' instead of repeating itself, then writes the result using only plain letters and digits so it can ride safely in an email.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC points to sections 3.10, 3.11, 3.15 and 4.2.10 for the security of content and of the decoding system, and says those points also apply to other encodings and attributes with similar functions. Those sections cover PEM, PGP, shell archives and the plain-text password attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parts of the parcel are locked, and some might contain commands. Be careful opening them, and do not run anything automatically.
